name: Noah's sleep, stress and the cold going round

parameters.label: Hours of sleep each night
parameters.explain: People sleeping under 6 hours were about 4 times more likely to catch a cold than those sleeping over 7.

parameters.label: Short nights in a row
parameters.explain: Ongoing short sleep weakens the body's defence; one late night does much less.

parameters.label: Sleep quality
parameters.explain: Restless, broken sleep rests the body less than the same hours of sound sleep.

parameters.label: Stress level
parameters.explain: Exam stress has been measured lowering the activity of immune cells in students.

parameters.label: Weeks the stress lasts
parameters.explain: Long-lasting stress (a month or more) clearly raises the risk of colds; short stressful spells matter much less.

parameters.label: Classmates with colds
parameters.explain: Colds are caused by viruses passed between people — no virus nearby, no cold.

overlay.caption: short sleep + stress → weaker defence → the cold going around gets through

explain.summary: Colds come from viruses passed around Noah's class — he can't catch one if nobody has it. Whether the virus wins depends on his defences. Night after night of short sleep is the biggest factor: under six hours, people are about four times more likely to catch a cold. Stress adds to it: exam stress lowers immune-cell activity, though stress that lasts a month or more matters much more than a single week.
rules: The cold needs a virus: more sick classmates means more chances to catch it; hand-washing cuts that.
Sleeping under 6–7 hours raises the odds about 4 times, building up over several nights.
Stress raises the odds too — a little for one stressful week, more for stress lasting a month or more.
Sleep and stress multiply together, so both at once are worse than either alone.

source.fact: Colds are caused by viruses, most often rhinoviruses, spread by droplets and contaminated surfaces.
Volunteers sleeping under 6 hours were 4.2 times, and under 5 hours 4.5 times, more likely to catch a cold from the same virus than those sleeping over 7.
Ongoing sleep deficiency can weaken the body's defence against common infections.
Stressors lasting a month or longer were linked to a much higher risk of colds; short stressful events were not.
In medical students, immune (natural killer) cell activity fell between a month before exams and the first day of exams.
Hand-washing reduces colds and other respiratory illnesses by 16–21%.
Teens need 8–10 hours of sleep a night.

choice.what: Short sleep's effect builds over 5 nights
choice.why: One late night matters less than a pattern; the study measured people's usual sleep over a week.

choice.what: A single stressful week raises risk only about a third as much as month-long stress
choice.why: Long stress is clearly linked to colds; the exam-stress study shows a smaller, short-term effect too.

choice.what: Each classmate with a cold adds about 2% to the starting chance
choice.why: A teaching number for 'more virus around, more chances'.

choice.what: Immune defence is shown as one percentage
choice.why: The real immune system has many parts; one number shows the direction.

illustrative: Noah's five hours, his stress level, the twelve sick classmates and the percentages are made up for a fictional story.
provenance.studying: Exactly how sleep and stress change the many parts of the immune system is still being worked out.

citations.title: About Common Cold
citations.supports: Colds are caused by viruses, most often rhinoviruses; they spread through droplets from coughs and sneezes and contaminated surfaces; colds usually last less than a week.

citations.title: Short Sleepers Are Four Times More Likely to Catch a Cold
citations.supports: In a study published in Sleep (2015), volunteers given cold virus by nose drops were 4.2 times more likely to catch a cold if they slept under 6 hours, and 4.5 times under 5 hours, than those sleeping over 7; this held after accounting for stress and other factors.

citations.title: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency: How Sleep Affects Your Health
citations.supports: During sleep the brain forms pathways to learn and remember; sleep-deficient people react more slowly, make more mistakes and have trouble focusing; ongoing sleep deficiency can weaken the body's defence against common infections.

citations.title: Types of stressors that increase susceptibility to the common cold in healthy adults (Health Psychology)
citations.supports: Severe stressors lasting a month or longer were linked to a substantial rise in the risk of catching a cold, while severe short stressful events (under a month) were not; there was some sign that longer stressors meant greater risk.

citations.title: Pillar articles: stress in humans affects natural killer cell function
citations.supports: Describes Kiecolt-Glaser and Glaser's study of 75 medical students: natural killer (immune) cell activity fell significantly between a month before final exams and the first day of exams, which the authors called a relatively minor stressor.

citations.title: Handwashing Facts
citations.supports: Handwashing education reduces respiratory illnesses such as colds in the general population by 16–21%.

citations.title: Sleep in Middle and High School Students
citations.supports: Teens aged 13–18 should get 8 to 10 hours of sleep per 24 hours (American Academy of Sleep Medicine); about 7 in 10 high schoolers don't get enough on school nights; short sleep is linked to attention problems.

does: Shows a cold needing both a virus and a weakened defence
Shows short sleep as the biggest single factor
Shows stress adding to it, more when it lasts longer
doesnt: Measure any real person — Noah is fictional
Predict whether anyone will get sick
Cover flu, other illnesses or what to do when sick
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Most colds pass in under a week. If you feel very unwell or it lasts much longer, tell an adult.
